beats.lead: The most famous demonstration that a computer understood gender and royalty
beats.note: No dictionary, no hand-coded rules — the model was never told what a king or a queen is.

beats.name: word2vec
beats.role: Tomas Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado and Jeffrey Dean at Google trained it purely by having it predict which words sit near each other across huge amounts of ordinary text.

beats.lead: The result got a name of its own.
beats.text: Take the vector for 'King', subtract 'Man', add 'Woman' — the closest vector left in the whole space is 'Queen.'
beats.note: That is the paper's own wording, not a paraphrase added later.

beats.context: The test set built to check this wasn't one lucky example — thousands of analogy questions, split between semantic pairs like king/queen and syntactic ones like big/biggest.

beats.lead: It didn't get them all right.
beats.text: The best version of the model answered about two in three correctly: 66.1% on semantic questions, 65.1% on syntactic ones.
beats.note: Genuinely impressive for 2013, and nowhere near solved.

beats.line: It never learned what a queen is. It learned where the word sits.
